lead: A sub-Boolean algebra is a smaller Boolean algebra sitting inside a given one. It must contain 0 and 1 and stay closed under join, meet and complement. A Boolean homomorphism is a map between Boolean algebras that preserves those three operations and both constants. These ideas exist to compare algebras and to recognise when a subset or an image behaves exactly like the whole. They appear in digital logic, where a small set of gates may generate a full switching algebra, and in database query systems, where filters form Boolean subalgebras. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.3 for lattice homomorphism and Chapter 5.5 for Boolean laws.

blocks.text: Let B be a Boolean algebra. A subset S⊆B is a sub-Boolean algebra when 0∈S, 1∈S, and for all a,b∈S, a∨b∈S, a∧b∈S and a′∈S. Some syllabi call S a Boolean subalgebra. The five conditions matter together. A sublattice needs only join and meet closure, so it can miss 0, 1 or complements. To test a candidate S: check 0 and 1; check every join of two elements; check every meet; check every complement. Stop when one check fails. Inside P({1,2,3}), where U={1,2,3}, S={∅,{1},{2,3},U} passes. For example {1}∨{2,3}=U and {1}∧{2,3}=∅. The set T={∅,{1},{2},{1,2,3}} fails because {1}∨{2}={1,2} is missing.
S is a sub-Boolean algebra ⇔ 0,1∈S and S is closed under ∨, ∧, ′
blocks.where: S⊆B; 0 and 1 are the constants of B; ′ is complement in B.

blocks.text: A Boolean homomorphism h:B→B₂ is a map that preserves all Boolean operations and constants. If h is bijective, it is a Boolean isomorphism. The image h(B) is always a sub-Boolean algebra of B₂. A lattice homomorphism may preserve ∨ and ∧ yet fail complement or constants, so it is not automatically a Boolean homomorphism. Test h(A)=1 when 1∈A, else 0, from P(U) to {0,1}. For join: h(A∪C)=1 iff 1∈A∪C iff 1∈A or 1∈C iff h(A)∨h(C)=1. Meet and complement follow similarly. h(∅)=0 and h(U)=1, so h is a Boolean homomorphism.

blocks.where: h:B→B₂; a,b∈B; operations on the right are in B₂.

spec.aria: Hasse diagram of the power set of {1,2,3}; the marked nodes ∅, 1, 23 and 123 form a sub-Boolean algebra.

examples.question: Let U={1,2,3}, B=P(U), S={∅,{1},{2,3},U}. (a) Show S is a sub-Boolean algebra of B. (b) For h:B→{0,1}, h(A)=1 if 1∈A else 0, use A={1,2} and C={2,3} to verify the join, meet and complement laws and the constants.
steps: Joins: {1}∨{2,3}=U; ∅∨X=X; X∨X=X. All are in S.
Meets: {1}∧{2,3}=∅; ∅∧X=∅; X∧X=X. All are in S.
Complements: ∅′=U, U′=∅, {1}′={2,3}, {2,3}′={1}. All are in S. So S is a sub-Boolean algebra.
These values verify the five identities for the chosen A and C; the general argument in Section 2 proves h is a Boolean homomorphism.
examples.answer: S is a sub-Boolean algebra; h is a Boolean homomorphism. The computed values: h(A)=1, h(C)=0, h(U)=1, h(A)∨h(C)=1, h({2})=0, h(A)∧h(C)=0, h(A′)=0, h(A)′=0, h(∅)=0, h(U)=1.

traps: Checking only join and meet closure. A sub-Boolean algebra also needs complement closure and both 0 and 1.
Forgetting that a Boolean homomorphism must send 0 to 0 and 1 to 1; a lattice homomorphism need not.
Confusing a sub-Boolean algebra with a sublattice: every sub-Boolean algebra is a sublattice, but not conversely.
Assuming h(B) must equal B₂. A homomorphism's image is only a sub-Boolean algebra of the codomain.

quiz.q: Define a sub-Boolean algebra of B.
quiz.a: A subset S⊆B with 0∈S, 1∈S, closed under ∨, ∧ and ′.

quiz.q: Why is T={∅,{1},{2},{1,2,3}} not a sub-Boolean algebra of P({1,2,3})?
quiz.a: {1}∨{2}={1,2} is missing from T, so join closure fails.

quiz.q: List the five identities a Boolean homomorphism h:B→B₂ must satisfy.
For h(A)=1 if 1∈A else 0 for U={1,2,3}, compute h({3}), h({1,3}), h(∅), h(U).
Show the image h(B) of a Boolean homomorphism is a sub-Boolean algebra of B₂.
quiz.a: It contains h(0)=0 and h(1)=1. It is closed because h(a)∨h(b)=h(a∨b), h(a)∧h(b)=h(a∧b), and h(a)′=h(a′).

quiz.q: Give a lattice homomorphism between Boolean algebras that is not a Boolean homomorphism.
quiz.a: Let h:B→{0,1} be the constant map h(x)=0. It preserves ∨ and ∧, but h(1)=0≠1.

quiz.q: Is h(A)=1 if 1∈A else 0 bijective for U={1,2,3}? Explain.
quiz.a: No. h({1})=1 and h({1,2})=1, so two inputs share one output.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every finite Boolean algebra is isomorphic to a power set algebra, which is the Stone representation theorem. Subalgebras appear as fields of sets in probability and as filter conditions in database queries. Boolean homomorphisms model translations between logic circuits and binary decision diagrams. Search 'Stone representation theorem', 'field of sets', 'Boolean subalgebra'.
